extracted.intended_audience: general readers seeking moral, financial, and practical self-improvement advice (18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short essays and letters giving practical rules of conduct, thrift, health, industry, and truthfulness intended to guide the behavior and habits of readers. The texts offer concrete maxims, examples, and short parables to teach personal finance, social conduct, and bodily regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: The good paymaster is lord of another man's purse
rubrics_metrics.description: He that is known to pay punctually and exactly to the time he promises, may at any time, and on any occasion, raise all the money his friends can spare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never keep borrowed money an hour beyond the time you promised, lest a disappointment shut up your friend's purse for ever. Punctual repayment raises credit and is often more useful than industry and frugality alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regard trifling actions that affect a man's credit
rubrics_metrics.description: The most trifling actions that affect a man's credit are to be regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small visible habits (e.g., the sound of your hammer at early/late hours) reassure creditors; being seen at a billiard-table or tavern when you should be at work may prompt immediate demands for payment. Appearances of industry and mindfulness increase credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep an exact account of expenses and income
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent thinking all you possess is your own, keep an exact account for some time both of your expenses and your income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention particulars at first to discover how small, trifling expenses mount up to large sums and discern what may be saved without great inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry and frugality as the fundamentals of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to wealth depends chiefly on two words, industry and frugality; waste neither time nor money, but make the best use of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He that gets all he can honestly, and saves all he gets (necessary expenses excepted), will certainly become rich unless providence decides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure food and drink to constitution and activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Eat and drink such an exact quantity as the constitution of thy body allows of, in reference to the services of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who study much ought not to eat as much as those who work hard; youth, age, the sick, and differing complexions require different quantities. Find the exact measure and keep it constantly; eat for necessity, not pleasure; labour to bring appetite to reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess in all things
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess in all other things whatever, as well as in meat and drink, is also to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A greater quantity of some foods may be eaten than others (lighter digestion), but the guiding rule is moderation tailored to individual constitution and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't give too much for the whistle (avoid needless expenditures and sacrifices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many miseries come from false estimates of the value of things and by giving too much for their whistles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whistle anecdote advises against paying more than the value of a thing and against sacrificing time, liberty, virtue, health, friends, or finances for fleeting objects like court favour, popularity, wealth, pleasure, or appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury can spur industry but may be harmful if it consumes necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: The hope of being one day able to purchase and enjoy luxuries is a spur to labour and industry; luxury may produce more than it consumes but can be a public evil when it displaces necessaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a fashionable cap induced local industry (knitting mittens) — a beneficial effect; but exporting victuals to import luxuries (rum, sugar) while populace lacks basic clothing/food is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ labour in useful work; avoid employment that produces nothing of lasting value
rubrics_metrics.description: The employment of men and women in works that produce neither the necessaries nor conveniences of life produces want and misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you feed people who do nothing useful (fiddling, entertainment that produces nothing), your wealth diminishes; prefer employing labourers in spinning, brickmaking, farming — productive work that preserves and increases wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness in trade builds credit; lying ruins reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no excuse for lying; truth in dealers raises credit and trade while falsehood drives customers away and ultimately ruins fortunes and reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and stories (Augustus honoring an honest enemy-priest; Pamphilius punished for lying) show social consequences. Liars cannot be trusted, will swear to falsehoods, and pose danger in private and public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and fair dealing attract customers and replace fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Dealers who are truthful, diligent, and probity make up with truth what they are deficient of in stock; their fair dealing brings customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people in trade judged rightly, haggling would be unnecessary and trust would simplify commerce; fair dealing raises credit which supplies lack of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay ready money when possible to avoid credit charges
rubrics_metrics.description: In buying goods, it is best to pay ready money because he that sells upon credit expects to lose five per cent by bad debts and charges an advance on credit sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who pay on credit share the cost of these advances; paying cash helps escape that extra charge and may be economically preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small wastes of time and money compound into large losses
rubrics_metrics.description: He that spends a groat a day idly, spends idly above six pounds a year; he that wastes a groat's worth of his time per day wastes the privilege of using a larger sum in trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wasting small amounts of money or time consistently leads to substantial losses over a lifetime; think of time lost as lost capital that could have been invested or turned to advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two simple rules to fill empty purses
rubrics_metrics.description: First, let honesty and industry be thy constant companions; and, secondly, spend one penny less than thy clear gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following these two rules will prevent creditors' insults, want, hunger, and nakedness; independence comes from saving a portion of clear gains while being honest and industrious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a fault-finding, querulous disposition (leave off looking at the ugly leg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sorts of people with equal comforts become happy or miserable by the different views they take; those who always notice the bad will be unhappy and disliked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not habitually criticise or dwell on inconveniences; doing so alienates friends, prevents support in public censure, and harms prospects. Learn to focus on conveniences and be pleasanter company.
